title: Greedy Algorithms
description: How Greedy Algorithms make locally-optimal choices without ever looking back -- fast and efficient, but not always correct.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A **Greedy Algorithm** repeatedly takes whatever looks best *right now* -- like grabbing the priciest item you can still fit at a buffet, no planning ahead.

Unlike brute force, it never explores every possibility -- it commits to one local decision and moves on, **no backtracking, no second-guessing**. That's exactly what makes it fast: no exponential search space, no big tables of intermediate results. Most greedy algorithms run in **O(n)** or **O(n log n)**.

sections.title: Why Greedy Algorithms Matter
sections.content:
Real systems -- flight gate scheduling, CPU task queues, GPS routing -- can't afford to test every possibility. Scheduling 100 tasks has 100! possible orderings (~9×10¹⁵⁷) -- far more than atoms in the universe. Exhaustive search is a non-starter; greedy is the practical alternative.

**GPS navigation** (Dijkstra's algorithm) greedily expands the nearest unvisited node. **Data compression** (Huffman coding) greedily merges the least-frequent characters. **Scheduling** (earliest-deadline-first) greedily picks the nearest deadline first.

sections.title: Core Idea of Greedy Algorithms
sections.content:
The pattern: look at your options, pick the locally best one, commit permanently, repeat until done.

Making 30 cents with US coins: take a quarter (25¢, 5¢ left), then a nickel (5¢) -- 2 coins, optimal.

Unlike Dynamic Programming, greedy doesn't backtrack or explore alternatives -- once chosen, a decision is final. It works precisely when a locally optimal choice leads to a globally optimal result. That's not guaranteed, which is why greedy is a *strategy*, not a universal fix.

sections.title: Local vs Global Optimization
sections.content:
**Local optimal** = the best immediate option. **Global optimal** = the best overall result. The tension between them is the whole challenge of greedy design.

Hiking uphill in the steepest direction (greedy) can strand you on a small local peak, missing the true summit hidden behind a ridge.

Coins `[1, 3, 4]`, target `6`: greedy takes 4 first (2 left), then two 1s -- 3 coins total. But **3 + 3 = 2 coins** is actually better. The greedy choice of 4 blocked it.

**Greedy works for:** canonical coin systems, Activity Selection, Minimum Spanning Tree, Huffman Coding, Dijkstra's (non-negative weights). **Greedy fails for:** arbitrary coin denominations, 0/1 Knapsack, Traveling Salesman.

sections.title: Greedy Choice Property
sections.content:
A problem is safely greedy-solvable if it has the **Greedy Choice Property**: a series of locally optimal choices reliably reaches the global optimum -- no backtracking or exploring alternatives needed.

**Activity Selection** is the textbook case: always pick the activity that finishes earliest. That leaves the most remaining time for everything else -- and it provably leads to the maximum number of activities scheduled.

Activity Selection, Huffman Coding, and Dijkstra's Algorithm all satisfy this property. Recognizing it is the key skill -- without it, greedy can quietly give you a wrong answer.

sections.title: Optimal Substructure
sections.content:
**Optimal substructure** means an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems -- shared by both greedy and Dynamic Programming.

Shortest path A→C through B: the A→B leg and B→C leg must each already be the shortest path for that segment.

The difference: greedy makes *one* choice and solves what's left. DP considers *multiple* choices and keeps the best. Together, Optimal Substructure (the problem breaks down cleanly) and the Greedy Choice Property (the local choice is provably safe) guarantee greedy reaches the global optimum.

sections.title: Coin Change Example
sections.content:
The classic example of greedy succeeding and failing on the same problem shape.

**Canonical system** `[10, 5, 1]`, target 18: take 10 (8 left), take 5 (3 left), take 1 three times → `[10,5,1,1,1]`, 5 coins -- optimal.

**Non-canonical** `[1, 3, 4]`, target 6: greedy takes 4 first (2 left), then two 1s → 3 coins. But `3 + 3` = 2 coins -- better. Greedy's early choice of 4 blocked it.

Greedy is safe for canonical systems (US and Euro coins qualify). For arbitrary denominations, use Dynamic Programming instead.

sections.title: Why Greedy Algorithms Are Fast
sections.content:
No exhaustive search, no backtracking, no testing every combination -- just commit and move on.

Activity Selection: brute force tries all 2ⁿ subsets (O(2^n)). Greedy sorts by end time (O(n log n)) then makes one linear scan (O(n)) -- exponentially faster overall.

Coin change (canonical): greedy is O(n) in the number of denominations. Brute force could be O(amount^n) -- infeasible for large amounts.

chart.title: Greedy algorithm efficiency
chart.description: Greedy avoids exhaustive exploration, scaling far better than brute-force search.

sections.title: When Greedy Algorithms Fail
sections.content:
Knowing when greedy fails matters as much as knowing when it works.

**Coin change (arbitrary denominations):** `[1,3,4]` target 6 -- greedy gives 3 coins, optimal is 2.

**0/1 Knapsack:** taking the best value-per-weight item first can leave unusable leftover capacity that two other items together would have filled better.

**Traveling Salesman (nearest-neighbor):** always visiting the closest unvisited city can produce a route far longer than optimal.

Greedy fails whenever the Greedy Choice Property doesn't hold -- a classic short-term-gain, long-term-pain trap.

sections.title: Greedy Algorithms vs Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
Greedy makes one irreversible choice per step. DP considers multiple choices and keeps the best.

Greedy: typically O(n) or O(n log n) time, O(1)-O(n) space. DP: typically O(n²) or O(n×W) time and space -- much heavier, but guarantees optimality where greedy can't.

**Use greedy** when the Greedy Choice Property holds and speed/memory matter most. **Use DP** when greedy fails or you need a guaranteed-optimal answer. Coin change: greedy for canonical systems, DP for arbitrary ones. Activity selection: greedy for maximizing count, DP if activities are weighted.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
Common greedy shape: sort, then make one pass, committing immediately to each choice.

**Coin selection:** sort coins descending, take as many of each as fit before moving to the next. **Largest-first:** repeatedly pull the max from a list (or just sort descending up front). **Greedy sum with a limit:** sort descending, add each value if it doesn't push the running sum past the limit.

codeSnippets.title: Simple greedy coin selection
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [10, 5, 1]
amount = 18
selected = []

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        selected.append(coin)
        amount -= coin

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Largest-first selection example
codeSnippets.code:
numbers = [3, 8, 2, 9, 5]
selected = []

while numbers:
    largest = max(numbers)
    selected.append(largest)
    numbers.remove(largest)

print(selected)

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
**Dijkstra's algorithm** greedily expands the nearest unvisited node for GPS routing. **Huffman coding** greedily merges the lowest-frequency characters for ZIP/JPEG compression.

**CPU scheduling:** Shortest-Job-First minimizes average wait; Earliest-Deadline-First serves real-time systems. **Prim's / Kruskal's** greedily add the cheapest edge that doesn't create a cycle -- network design's Minimum Spanning Tree.

Even without a full optimality guarantee, greedy often gives a fast, close-to-optimal approximation -- valuable when waiting for a perfect answer just isn't an option.

subsections.title: Misconception: Greedy Algorithms always find the best solution
subsections.content: The `[1,3,4]` coin counterexample proves otherwise. Always check the Greedy Choice Property before trusting greedy's answer.

subsections.title: Misconception: Greedy Algorithms are random shortcuts
subsections.content: Greedy is fully deterministic, based on a specific criterion -- largest coin, earliest finish time, smallest frequency. No randomness involved.

subsections.title: Misconception: Fast algorithms are always greedy
subsections.content: Binary Search and Merge Sort are Divide and Conquer, not greedy. Greedy is one strategy among several for efficient algorithms.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Works reliably only when a problem has the **Greedy Choice Property**.
**Fast and memory-efficient** -- usually O(n) or O(n log n).
Does **not always guarantee** the optimal solution.
Knowing when greedy works is the real skill.
